title: Reversible Atlantic overturning despite continued Greenland ice sheet melt
abstract: The Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC) is considered vulnerable to irreversible weakening or collapse under global warming and related Greenland ice sheet (GrIS) melt, yet its resilience to either forcing remains poorly constrained. Here, we use a carbon dioxide emission-driven Earth system model with an interactive GrIS to assess AMOC reversibility under a range of idealized carbon dioxide emission pathways that produce near-linear global warming up to 10 kelvins (K), stabilization across 1.5 to 9 K, and subsequent cooling. We find that although the AMOC reaches threshold-defined collapsed states, these do not represent dynamical tipping in this model: The overturning weakens quasi-linearly with global mean temperature increase yet consistently and promptly recovers under cooling. In contrast, GrIS mass loss accelerates with warming, continues through stabilizations, and is only slowed by cooling, committing the planet to long-term sea level rise. These results reveal contrasting resilience across climate system components: Under transient carbon dioxide forcing, AMOC strength remains dynamically reversible despite continued Greenland meltwater input, whereas the GrIS is locked into persistent decline. Our findings underscore the urgency of rapid emission cuts to limit climate overshoot, AMOC weakening, and irreversible ice sheet loss.

title: Lead isotope evidence for Antarctic Ice Sheet changes in the Weddell Sea sector since the Last Glacial Maximum
abstract: The Weddell Sea influences global ocean circulation and sea level through modulating Antarctic Bottom Water formation and Antarctic Ice Sheet discharges, but the history of ice‐sheet dynamics in this region remains poorly constrained due to limited well‐dated geological records. To provide a new geochemical perspective on ice‐sheet dynamics since the Last Glacial Maximum (LGM), this study presents paired authigenic and detrital Pb isotope records from sediment core PS1599‐3 recovered from the continental slope north of the Filchner Trough. Comparison with Antarctic Pb isotope provinces indicates that both detrital and authigenic Pb signatures were possibly sourced from a Shackleton Range‐like region in the south‐eastern Weddell Sea sector of East Antarctica. This suggests that dominant upstream drainage sources remained broadly stable throughout the last ~23 ka. We interpret the downcore Pb isotope variations to primarily reflect changes in the delivery of subglacial weathering‐derived Pb associated with grounding‐line dynamics in the Filchner Trough. Authigenic 206 Pb/ 204 Pb ratios show a sharp increase at ~23 ka, followed by two decreases at ~20 and 11–9 ka. We suggest that a re‐advance of grounded ice near the LGM was followed by initial retreat at ~20 ka and further grounding‐line retreat or reorganization during the Early Holocene. These findings highlight the use of authigenic Pb isotopes as potential tracers for reconstructing polar ice‐sheet dynamics and meltwater influences.

title: The role of upper–deep ocean heat exchange in shaping warming patterns and climate feedbacks in CMIP6 models
abstract: Abstract Surface warming patterns modulate climate feedbacks. Ocean heat exchange redistributes heat between the upper and deep ocean, shaping warming patterns. However, its influence on climate feedbacks remains unclear. We explore this issue in the CMIP6 abrupt-4×CO2 experiment by dividing the simulation into fast, intermediate and slow phases and using an effective upper–deep ocean heat exchange coefficient (γ) inferred from a two-layer energy balance model. The intermediate phase stands out as the period when ocean heat exchange leaves its strongest imprint on warming patterns and climate feedbacks. Models with stronger ocean heat exchange (high-γ ensemble) differ from those with weaker exchange (low-γ ensemble) in both background ocean state and response, exhibiting weaker mean-state stratification and a stronger Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC) favoring stronger heat penetration, subsurface warming, and distinct warming pattern and feedback evolution. Across the three phases, the low-γ ensemble sustains intensified warming in the tropical eastern Pacific and Southern Ocean alongside subdued warming in the Northern Hemisphere extratropics. However, the high-γ ensemble experiences a warming pattern reversal over these regions, tied to stronger intermediate-phase heat penetration and AMOC weakening. This centennial-scale warming pattern reversal, overlooked in previous work, partly mirrors the millennial-scale reversal previously found in multi-millennial abrupt-4×CO2 simulations. The high-γ ensemble also exhibits a larger increase and later peak change in net climate feedback. These findings highlight ocean heat exchange and associated ocean mean-state differences as key controls on time-evolving warming patterns and climate feedbacks.

title: Seasonal icings reveal subsurface water drainage of a Greenland Ice Sheet outlet glacier
abstract: Ice cores from Isunnguata Sermia’s forefield reveal how proglacial naled and accreted ices form in Greenland. Naledi build up in winter from precipitation and mineral-rich subglacial water, while accreted ice forms in summer through supercooled water upwelling. Geophysical surveys indicate both are fed by subsurface flows potentially originating from the glacier bed. Here, we present the first conceptual model of these formations in Greenland.

title: Holocene millennial climate variability influenced by tropical–Antarctic ocean–atmosphere interactions
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
abstract: A prominent unstable feature, millennial-scale climate oscillation (MCO), punctuated the Holocene. Solar activity and deep ocean variability are generally regarded as the origin of the MCO, yet the dynamics remain debated. Using a Holocene transient simulation with the EC-Earth climate model (8 to 0 ka BP), together with a global compilation of 304 temperature reconstructions, here we identify a robust ~1,350-y oscillatory mode that characterizes Holocene climate variability and is self-sustained and crucially influenced by tropical–Antarctic ocean–atmosphere interactions. Within each cycle, Antarctic Bottom Water (AABW) strengthening evolves with the developing warming and an El Niño-like tropical sea surface temperature (SST) response, accompanied by anticyclonic circulation anomalies over the high-latitude Southern Ocean. Northward cold advection of the associated enhanced westerly winds off the Antarctic coast overcomes the effect of sea ice retreat to promote AABW formation, ocean stratification, and warming. Positive feedbacks including sea ice-albedo, tropical air–sea interaction, and SST-AABW magnify surface warming till AABW reaches its peak. Thereafter, reduced brine rejection from sea-ice retreat weakens AABW, counteracts the warming, and commences a switch to its cooling phase. The dominant periodicity, consistent with that inferred from proxy reconstructions, is confirmed by complementary climate simulations. These results provide an alternative physical mechanism for Holocene millennial-scale climate variability. Under future anthropogenic warming, a positive phase of the oscillation may heighten the positive feedbacks, thereby increasing the risk of rapid climate transformation.

title: Holocene water mass structure changes in Lake Nurume, Lützow-Holm Bay, East Antarctica
journal: Progress in Earth and Planetary Science
abstract: Abstract Paleoenvironmental reconstructions using sediments from isolation basins including lakes are useful approaches to obtain evidence of sea-level and ice-sheet changes in Antarctica. However, a detailed study using multiple sediment cores of how isolation basins respond to external forcings is needed to improve the accuracy of paleoenvironmental reconstructions. We reconstructed how the water mass structure of Lake Nurume, located in Langhovde, Lützow-Holm Bay, East Antarctica, changed in response to sea-level and ice-sheet changes during the Holocene using sediments from different water depths and nearby trenches. Sedimentary observations, diatom analyses, and X-ray fluorescence core scanner analyses were conducted to reconstruct the three-dimensional characterization of water mass structure combined with the paleotopographic reconstruction using glacial isostatic adjustment modelling. Sedimentation resumed at approximately 6.6 cal kyr BP when the lake became ice-free and marine conditions, as evidenced by the presence of marine diatoms and shell fossils. At approximately 2.0 cal kyr BP, laminated structures appeared in sediment cores, accompanied by a decrease in benthic diatoms. This transition is interpreted as a response to ice-sheet readvance, whereby the ice margin approached the lake, increasing freshwater input and reducing vertical mixing. The resulting stratification caused anoxic conditions in the bottom water. Finally, at approximately 0.5 cal kyr BP, the lake became completely isolated from the sea, establishing its current water mass structure. These findings contribute to more accurate paleoenvironmental reconstructions such as sea-level and ice-sheet changes using sediments from isolation basins in Antarctica.

title: Transition to a much warmer climate for the global ocean and Antarctic Ice Sheet coupled system, and its reversibility
abstract: How the Antarctic ice sheet responds to rapid ocean warming remains uncertain. To explore this, we used a coupled ocean–ice sheet model. We compared simulations under present-day conditions with simulations under strong future warming for 50 years, then returned to today's climate. The ocean warmed quickly but recovered within decades. In contrast, several ice streams continued to retreat for centuries. This shows that even brief warming could cause lasting ice loss and sea-level rise.

title: Rate-induced tipping of ice sheets due to visco-elastic Earth response under idealized conditions
abstract: Here we examine the tipping dynamics of instability-prone marine ice sheets in interaction with the underlying solid Earth in a simplified model setup. The idealized ensemble simulations allow a systematic investigation of (1) bifurcation-induced and (2) rate-induced ice-sheet tipping for a wide range of representative Antarctic solid-Earth structures. We examine the conditions that lead to shifts in the tipping thresholds, the occurrence of rate-induced tipping or grounding-line overshoots.

title: Forçamento orbital e assimetria hemisférica da insolação no pleistoceno-holoceno
abstract: This study models the seasonal and latitudinal redistribution of orbital insolation for five Pleistocene-Holocene periods: MIS 11 (~400 ka), the Last Interglacial (~125 ka), the Last Glacial Maximum (~21 ka), the early Holocene (~11.7 ka), and the present (0 ka BP = 1950 CE), across nine latitudes from 65°S to 65°N. ORBIT91 parameters were used to calculate Earth-Sun distance, solar declination, photoperiod, and daily top-of-atmosphere insolation. At 65°N during the June solstice, Q ranged from 466.0 W m⁻² in MIS 11 to 537.4 W m⁻² in the Last Interglacial. During austral summer, however, the present has the highest value among the analyzed periods at 40°S, 60°S, and 65°S; at 65°S it reaches 510.9 W m⁻², about 7% above the present-day peak at 65°N. The current precessional configuration, with perihelion near the December solstice, explains this asymmetry. The caloric summer metric, surface-energy scenarios, and comparison with FAO-56 complement the analysis. The results frame insolation as a seasonal forcing capable of modulating hemispheric energy contrasts, whose climatic expression depends on atmospheric circulation and Earth-system feedbacks. The transmittance and evaporation scenarios represent idealized energy bounds rather than observed or reconstructed surface-climate conditions.

title: Latitudinal Heterogeneity in South Asian Monsoon Changes Since the Last Glacial Maximum Revealed by Ganga–Brahmaputra Vegetation Record
abstract: Abstract Future changes in South Asian climate are expected to amplify flooding and drought, yet the spatial and temporal variability of the South Asian monsoon (SAM) under different climate regimes remains poorly constrained. Here, we present a new marine pollen record from the Bay of Bengal (BoB), informing on the vegetation of the Ganges‐Brahmaputra (G‐B) River basin whose outlet via the lower Meghna lies near 21.3°–21.8°N, and compare it with bulk and leaf‐wax δ 13 C and δD, and planktonic foraminiferal δ 18 O records, all from the same site. The G‐B basin was characterized by an open landscape with sparse subtropical trees during Marine Isotope Stage (MIS) 2 indicating drier and colder conditions. This is in sharp contrast with the development of tropical forests during MIS 1. During the Holocene, changes in the forest composition, characterized by a progressive increase in dry tropical trees relative to moist taxa, showed large‐scale drying, with more pronounced winter dryness after 8 ka. The comparison with the pollen records located off Mahanadi (20°N) and Godavari (18°N) catchments, both within the Indian core monsoon zone reveals that the composition of the forests differs strongly, showing a persistent north–south hydroclimate gradient. At orbital time scales, vegetation records from the western BoB support that the SAM variability is intrinsically linked to the ITCZ migration and largely affected by the Northern hemisphere ice‐sheets and insolation forcing; this is particularly significant for the Holocene. However, the spatial heterogeneity of hydroclimate conditions suggests additional modulation by Himalayan orography, and vegetation through moisture recycling.

title: The overshoot integral can inform climate science and policy beyond 1.5 °C of warming
abstract: Abstract The carbon budget framework has served as the dominant organising principle for climate science and policy, linking cumulative emissions to peak warming and providing a tractable scalar constraint for international negotiations. With 1.5 °C exceedance now imminent and virtually all mitigation scenarios involving substantial temperature overshoot before net-negative emissions could return temperatures to target, the budget framework’s utility for evaluating and minimising risk generated by warming risks becoming diminished. We propose a complementary organising principle: the overshoot integral, defined as the time-integrated temperature exceedance above a policy-relevant threshold, with units of °C·years. Analogous to degree-heating weeks in coral bleaching prediction and positive degree-days in glaciology, the overshoot integral captures both the magnitude and duration of exceedance in a single scalar quantity. Applying this metric to future climate pathways, we show that pathways with similar peak temperatures can differ by more than two orders of magnitude in their cumulative degree-year burden. Applied to CMIP7 ScenarioMIP/FaIR (Finite Amplitude Impulse Response simple climate model) trajectories, calculating overshoot integrals reveal substantial differences in cumulative thermal exposure across pathways. For Earth-system impacts whose response dynamics integrate forcing over time, spanning marine habitat, permafrost carbon and mountain glaciers, we show that cumulative thermal exposure captured by the overshoot integral contains impact-relevant information not captured by peak warming alone. A simple risk formulation combining peak and cumulative exposure improves out-of-sample prediction across all three systems. That the overshoot integral is best understood not as a reversible account that can be debited and credited, but as a cumulative dose should inform climate policy and science in the increasingly warmer future.

title: Atmospheric stabilization of the East Antarctic ice sheet under warming
abstract: Nature Climate Change, Published online: 30 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41558-026-02791-x The long-term response of the Greenland and Antarctic ice sheets to warming is often studied using ice-only simulations. Here the authors use a coupled ice–atmosphere–ocean model and find that East Antarctica remains stable even under higher warming because changes in atmospheric circulation increase precipitation sensitivity.

title: The uncertain impacts of an 1.5 °C overshoot-and-decline scenario on carbon stocks and productivity in terrestrial ecosystems
abstract: Abstract Overshoot scenarios, in which global temperatures peak and then decline through emission reductions and CO 2 removal, are increasingly central to climate policy as we are already approaching 1.5 °C warming. Yet the ecological reversibility of such pathways remains poorly understood, even though the trajectories of productivity and carbon stocks in terrestrial ecosystems have major implications for land-based carbon sink projections. Here we draw on four complementary lines of research to study the land carbon sink under overshoot: (i) CMIP6 models project declines in net ecosystem productivity (NEP) after peak warming. Nevertheless, NEP remains positive, leading to a stabilisation of the carbon stocks in terrestrial vegetation (cVeg). The CO 2 ramp up-down model experiment by CDRMIP underscores that these models predict near-reversibility of the vegetation carbon stock. (ii) A systematic review on global change experiments identified 256 papers (warming, drought, irrigation or elevated CO 2 , all elements of an overshoot scenario). However, only 15 included a recovery phase following treatment. This reveals a gap in experimental design for understanding ecosystem responses under overshoot conditions. Where recovery was assessed, responses were mixed, with persistent legacy effects documented after drought. (iii) Modern-day overshoot analogues, including two El Niño events and the 2018–2020 European droughts, show that compound heat and drought can cause carbon losses that recover slowly, with repeated extremes progressively reducing ecosystem resilience. (iv) Paleoclimate records from the Holocene Climatic Optimum and the Paleocene–Eocene Thermal Maximum demonstrate that exceeding ecological thresholds can trigger vegetation changes and carbon cycle feedbacks that long outlast the climatic perturbation itself. Together, these findings show that the trajectory of the terrestrial carbon sink during climate overshoot is uncertain, because ecosystem responses are often delayed, nonlinear, and threshold dependent.

title: Workshop report: Lake KINneret Drilling (KIND) – reconstructing Pliocene–Quaternary hydroclimate and seismic history of the Levant
abstract: The southern Levant extends between the hyperarid Sahara–Arabia Desert belt in the south and the temperate Mediterranean climate zone in the north, making the regional hydroclimate extremely sensitive to even small perturbations of global climate. The region further served as a major pathway for the “out-of-Africa” dispersal of fauna, flora, and hominins throughout the Quaternary, as well as for human cultural development from the Paleolithic to the Neolithic. Spanning the length of the Levant is the Dead Sea Transform (DST) that transfers the opening at the Red Sea in the south to the collision at the Taurus Mountains in the north. Pull-apart basins along the DST host the hypersaline Dead Sea and freshwater Lake Kinneret, whose sedimentary records document the regional hydroclimate and seismic history. Lake Kinneret (a.k.a. the Sea of Galilee) is the largest freshwater lake in the Levant, whose precursors have deposited a thick sequence of lacustrine sediments since the late Miocene. Seismic profiles across the tectonically subsiding basin in the middle of the modern lake, as well as existing short sediment cores, indicate that the sedimentary sequences are generally bounded by two N–S-striking longitudinal faults and generally maintain stratigraphic order. The sedimentary column is dominated by primary authigenic calcite, whose chemical and isotopic composition documents regional hydrology and lacustrine conditions from at least the Pliocene. Accordingly, the sedimentary record of Lake Kinneret holds the potential to serve as one of the longest and most highly resolved lacustrine records since the Pliocene, yielding sub-centennial records of hydroclimate, paleoseismicity, geomagnetism, and paleobotanics in a region of fundamental importance for the global understanding of climate change, tectonics, and human evolution. The Lake KINneret Drilling (KIND) project aims to establish an exceptionally long Pliocene–Quaternary chronostratigraphic reference record that will contribute to a meridional synthesis of continental and marine core records along the East African Rift–Dead Sea Transform (EARDST) corridor. Owing to its location, the KIND record will yield transformative contributions to climate modeling and to our understanding of climate change in the eastern Mediterranean, a recognized global warming “hotspot”. Moreover, it will document seismic activity along the DST over long timescales, providing a basis for policymakers to prepare for this potential major hazard to infrastructure and human life. Taken together, the KIND project will provide unique and much-needed records from a tectonically active region that is projected to become increasingly arid over the coming century and that is already burdened by severe geopolitical strife. These records are critical for identifying and quantifying regional climate change patterns, assessing seismic risks, and evaluating the ecological impacts of these processes.

title: Imaging the Ross Ice Streams of West Antarctica using active source seismology
abstract: Preprint under review for ESSD (discussion: open, 0 comments) Knowledge of the past and future of Earth's ice sheets requires us to image beneath the ice surface and into the ice, water, sediment, and rock that lies beneath. An effective way of doing this uses active source seismology. Here we present active source seismic data imaging a diverse range of subglacial environments including subglacial lakes, sub-ice ocean cavities, and geological archives preserving the history of the ice sheets.

Climate variability and human adaptation in late quaternary Northeast Asia: A critical review of paleoenvironmental and archaeological records from Northeast China and Primorye of Russia
abstract: Northeast China and Russian Primorye lie at the confluence of the East Asian summer monsoon, Siberian High, and Pacific maritime circulation. The region experienced pronounced glacial-interglacial variability and served as a corridor for human dispersal among Siberia, East Asia, and the Americas. This review synthesises palaeoecological and archaeological evidence, principally from the past ca. 50 ka. Environmental records trace a transition from the cold, arid steppe of the Last Glacial Maximum (ca. 26.5–19.0 ka BP) to warmer, more forested Holocene landscapes, while revealing strong spatial heterogeneity and abrupt events. Although the ≥146 ka Harbin cranium predates the main review interval, it establishes a Middle Pleistocene hominin presence; securely dated archaeological sequences considered here begin in the Late Pleistocene. These records document developments from Upper Palaeolithic lithic industries to Neolithic sedentism, millet agriculture, and Bronze Age sociopolitical complexity. A central limitation is the spatial separation of most palaeoclimatic archives and archaeological sites. Their differing chronological resolution further restricts direct causal attribution, leaving many proposed climate-culture relationships as working hypotheses. We therefore advocate co-located multiproxy transects, improved chronological control, and tephrochronological correlation. A site-by-site appraisal of radiocarbon, OSL, and U-series chronologies identifies relationships that are currently testable. The Boisman-Krounovka sequence suggests that resource breadth and specialisation may mediate vulnerability to environmental change, although the roles of social organisation, mobility, and demography remain unresolved. Northeast Asia thus offers a framework for generating and testing hypotheses about climatic variability, demographic processes, and cultural change rather than demonstrating simple climate-driven causation.

title: Late Quaternary lake filling and drying in northern Australia's largest freshwater lake
abstract: ABSTRACT Lake Woods, Jurrkulu, is northern Australia's largest freshwater lake filled today in strong Indo–Australian summer monsoons (IASM) to maximum depths of ~5 m. On the western margins of the lake, two large arcuate ridges occur 20 to 40 m above the lake floor and inset within these are other mid‐elevation lake deposits, such as depositional ridges, which suggest past filling events much higher than the modern maximum. We have undertaken the analysis of 20 samples for single‐grain optically stimulated luminescence (OSL) from shoreline and lake‐floor deposits and supplemented this chronology with an analysis of the basin hypsometry, basin‐wide erosion rates and rare earth elements to ascertain the dominant source of the large source‐bordering ridges. The outer and inner arcuate ridges represent both aeolian accumulation and inferred lake‐level highstands due to the presence of fine gravel facies and gastropods contained within them. We document two lake highstands at 195 ± 16 ka and at 98 ± 7 ka (20 and 15 m above the lake floor, respectively; the lake floor is 197 m Australian Height Datum, AHD). We also present a third but undated filling event 18.5 m above the lake floor (215.5 m AHD) but that is bracketed by two OSL ages of 91 ± 5 and 52 ± 3 ka, with a Bayesian modelled boundary age for lake filling of 95.9 to 53.8 ka (95% credible interval; C.I.). We find no evidence of the previously reported late Marine Isotope Stage [MIS] 3 highstand deposits and the prevalence of gully‐filled structureless sediments, dated to the mid to late Holocene, many of which contain archaeological artefacts that do not allow for the quantification of any accurate Holocene lake‐filling episodes. The lake floor is characterised by deeply cracking silts and clays, with single‐grain OSL results supporting significant post‐depositional mixing (maximum ages are <143 ka). Denudation rate data from detrital stream sediment samples indicate some of the lowest rates of denudation in northern Australia, of between 2.05 ± 0.51 and 0.83 ± 0.23 m/Myr, with the latter rate stemming from the dominant catchment area in the Barkly Tablelands. Sediment provenance data indicate that the slowly eroding Barkly Tablelands is the dominant source for the clays and silts in the lake basin. Despite being the largest lake in northern Australia, the slow rates of catchment‐wide erosion coupled with the intermittent filling have only produced a discontinuous record of the IASM, but one that shows exceptional episodic filling in MIS 5 to 4.

title: Merging Regional Climate Models and Remote Sensing Observations to Better Estimate Mountain Snow Water Equivalent
abstract: Abstract Large‐scale, high‐resolution estimation of snow water equivalent (SWE) in mountainous regions remains challenging. Continental‐scale approaches, including SWE reconstruction and regional climate model (RCM) simulations, are computationally expensive at high resolutions. We present Blender, a variational data assimilation method that improves modeled SWE and snowfall time series by modifying snowpack mass and energy balance while minimizing changes to input precipitation and energy fluxes, subject to remotely sensed snow cover fraction constraints. Blender combines the advantages of RCM simulation and SWE reconstruction and can be applied as a post‐processing step to many gridded snow data sets. We tested Blender at 500 m resolution in the Tuolumne watershed, Sierra Nevada, USA, during water years 2013, 2016, and 2017 (low, average, and high snow accumulation). We tested Blender with prior inputs from an RCM and ERA5‐Land (ERA5L), and evaluated posterior (output) performance using 18 Airborne Snow Observatory (ASO) flights, and compared its performance with the Western United States Snow Reanalysis (WUS‐SR). Blender improved spatial SWE patterns relative to ASO in all years for the RCM prior (RMSEP: 17.2% → 11.5%, R : 0.39 → 0.72) and ERA5L prior (RMSEP: 13.9% → 12.9%, R : 0.003 → 0.59), approaching WUS‐SR performance (RMSEP = 9.5%, R = 0.82). Blender improved snow water storage (SWS) estimates for the RCM prior but not for ERA5L prior, although ERA5L posterior SWS remained reasonably accurate (median absolute error of 27%). Blender provides a flexible and efficient pathway toward higher‐resolution, large‐scale SWE estimation in mountainous regions.

title: Reduced Evapotranspiration Decreases Land Precipitation Despite Enhanced Moisture Convergence: Insights from Perturbed Parameter Ensembles of Earth System Models
abstract: Abstract Both canonical theory and climate model simulations predict an increase in globally averaged precipitation with radiatively-forced warming. However, terrestrial processes control surface water and energy fluxes, and therefore can impact surface temperatures independently of radiative forcing. Here, we investigate the sensitivity of the global hydrological cycle to warming induced by changes in land surface conditions using perturbed parameter ensembles from two climate models, which sample a broad range of evapotranspiration (ET) states through modifications to land model parameters. The parameters are perturbed within the range of observationally constrained uncertainty and alter ET through different land surface pathways. We find that reduced ET drives warming yet decreases land-mean precipitation, which we link to strong decreases in near-surface relative humidity from warming. These decreases in relative humidity overcome increases in specific humidity and moisture convergence over land, which are also caused by shifts in large-scale circulation. We explain the tropical precipitation response to ET forcing with a simple scaling that relates changes in the land-ocean contrast in relative humidity to land-mean precipitation change. Further, the suppressed ET induces a shortwave cloud response that amplifies warming. Our results highlight that changes to land surface properties at the magnitude of parametric uncertainty influence warming and precipitation. ET-driven warming reduces land precipitation, opposite in sign to the precipitation increase from radiatively-forced warming. This response is not directly captured by scalings of the global hydrological cycle with radiative forcing. We therefore establish the potential significance of terrestrial ecosystem functioning, and its response to climate change, for hydroclimate.

title: Investigating the transition in ice dynamics from a land- to lake-terminating glacier using a simple glacier dynamics model
abstract: As climate change creates new lakes at the front of retreating glaciers, these ice bodies often accelerate and lose mass more quickly. We used a computer model to study this process at an Icelandic glacier. Our results show that thinning ice is the main driver for recent acceleration, with 37 % of the total ice loss resulting from the presence of the lake. These findings imply that as lakes grow globally, glaciers could vanish more rapidly than predicted, enhancing the rate of sea level rise.

title: The internal variability modulates marine heatwave duration changes by day-to-day ocean memory in the recent decades
abstract: Abstract The duration of marine heatwaves (MHWs) determines the cumulative thermal stress imposed on marine organisms, thereby strongly influencing the severity of ecological consequences. Recently, day-to-day ocean memory, quantified by a first-order sea surface temperature (SST) autocorrelation model, has been found as an effective metric to depict the duration of MHWs, due to its consistent climatological distribution and trends with MHW duration in the observations. However, the relative importance of external forcing and internal variability in modulating the day-to-day ocean memory and, more importantly, its relationship with MHW duration, remain unclear. In this study, we employ 100 ensemble members of CESM2 and 32 CMIP6 models to analyze the roles of external forcing and internal variability in the day-to-day ocean memory and MHW duration. We find that internal variability dominates the trends of day-to-day ocean memory in the recent decades and further modulates the trends of MHW duration, particularly in the tropical oceans. The zonal gradient of SST trends over the tropical Pacific emerges as a key feature of the internal variability. By combining a stochastic climate model framework with a mixed-layer heat budget, we further reveal that ocean mixing and dynamics are the primary processes through which internal variability modulates trends in day-to-day ocean memory, whereas SST-surface heat flux feedback provides a secondary contribution and variations in mixed-layer depth play negligible roles. This study demonstrates that internal variability exerts a considerable influence on MHW duration through its modulation on day-to-day ocean memory, providing crucial evidence and a new perspective for understanding and predicting MHW duration in a warming climate.

title: Climate Change and the Stability of Glacier-Fed River Systems: Implications for Water Security in Vulnerable Regions
journal: Journal of Climate Change and Environmental Coordination
abstract: This study examines how climate change is reshaping the stability of glacier fed river systems and the implications for water security in vulnerable regions. Glaciers function as natural water storage, moderating seasonal and interannual variability, yet rising temperatures and altered precipitation regimes are accelerating glacier retreat worldwide. Using an integrated methodological framework combining climate data, glacier mass balance modelling, hydrological simulation, and water security indicators, the study assesses observed and projected changes in river flow magnitude, timing, variability, and extremes across glacier dependent basins. Results show widespread and persistent glacier mass loss, with short term increases in meltwater runoff followed by long term declines in river discharge as ice reserves diminish. Seasonal peak flows are shifting earlier in the year, while late season low flows are becoming more pronounced, reducing flow reliability during periods of high demand. Increased interannual variability and more frequent hydrological extremes further undermine river system stability. These changes translate directly into declining water availability, reduced predictability, and heightened risk for agriculture, hydropower generation, domestic supply, and aquatic ecosystems. The discussion highlights strong spatial differences driven by climatic setting, glacier characteristics, and governance capacity, demonstrating that vulnerability is unevenly distributed across regions. The findings underscore the limitations of water management frameworks based on historical conditions and emphasize the need for adaptive and forward-looking strategies. By explicitly linking cryospheric change to river stability and water security, this study informs climate hydrology research and supports policy planning adaptation.

title: Miocene−Pliocene Nenana Gravel deposition in response to tectonic denudation of the Alaska Range (USA)
abstract: Disentangling the effects of tectonics and Pliocene−Pleistocene climate forcing on rates of erosion remains key to understanding hypothesized feedbacks among these processes. In central Alaska (United States), deposition of the Nenana Gravel has long been attributed to foreland basin sedimentation coupled to tectonically controlled Miocene−Pliocene Alaska Range exhumation. However, recent cosmogenic burial dating of the lower Nenana Gravel implies that deposition did not begin until ca. 2.3 Ma, consistent with Alaska Range erosion driven by concurrent intensified glaciation during Pleistocene global climate changes. Our new 3.67 ± 0.75 Ma cosmogenic 26Al/10Be isochron burial age at the top of the Nenana Gravel exposed at the Suntrana section indicates that deposition concluded ∼1 m.y. before the previously reported onset. We show that the prior data do not support early Pleistocene burial, but instead yield a 5.5 ± 1.5 Ma simple 26Al/10Be burial age of initial Nenana Gravel deposition, consistent with tephrochronologically constrained 6.7 ± 0.1 Ma strata that conformably underlie the gravel. Deposition of the ∼800-m-thick Nenana Gravel exposed at the Suntrana section thus started between 6.7 ± 0.1 Ma and 5.5 ± 1.5 Ma and concluded by 3.67 ± 0.75 Ma, concurrent with increased Alaska Range exhumation rates associated with tectonic forcing at ca. 7−6 Ma. The Nenana Gravel therefore records Alaska Range denudation induced by Miocene−Pliocene tectonics, and not early Pleistocene climate.

title: EnsAI: an emulator for atmospheric ammonia ensembles
abstract: EnsAI is a newly developed artificial intelligence based program for efficiently generating ensembles of atmospheric surface ammonia concentrations that can be used in emissions inversions systems. Ensemble-based data assimilation methods are widely used for assimilation and emissions inversions, but are usually very computationally demanding. Once trained, EnsAI can run thousands of times faster than the physics-based models when run on graphics processing units.

title: EnsAI: An Emulator for Atmospheric Ammonia Ensembles
abstract: arXiv:2504.16024v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Ensemble-based methods for data assimilation and emissions inversions are a popular way to encode flow-dependency within the model error covariance. While most ensemble methods do not require the use of an adjoint model, the need to repeatedly run a geophysical model to generate the ensemble can be a significant computational burden. In this paper, we introduce EnsAI, a new AI-based ensemble generation system for surface ammonia concentrations. When trained on an ensemble for ammonia generated by the GEM-MACH air quality model, it was shown that the ensembles produced by EnsAI can accurately reproduce the meteorology-dependent features of the original ensemble, while generating the ensemble 3,300 times faster than the original GEM-MACH ensemble. While EnsAI requires an upfront cost for generating the ensemble used for training, as well as the training itself, the long term computational savings can greatly exceed these initial computational costs. When used in an emissions inversion system, EnsAI produced similar inversion results to those in which the original GEM-MACH ensemble was used while using significantly less computational resources.

title: Volcanic impacts on East Asian climate since 1400: insights from climate reconstructions and paleoclimate reanalysis
journal: Geografiska Annaler Series A Physical Geography
abstract: This study analysed volcanic impacts on East Asian temperature and precipitation (wetness/dryness) anomalies and investigated the consistency of climate responses between the REACHES reconstruction and paleoclimate reanalysis product (ModE-RA) from the 15th to 20th centuries. Volcanic events were compiled from the eruption chronology based on ice-core sulphate data, and 10 major eruption events were identified. For each event, the eruption year was designated as t0 and used as the reference year for event alignment. Superposed epoch analysis was applied with a ± 8-year window to compare post-eruption years (t = 0–8) against pre-eruption baselines (t = −8–−1) by a significance t-test. For identifying whether extreme years (percentile thresholds from the top 5%–25% in temperature and precipitation fields) are attributed to volcanic forcing or natural variability, we adopted Bayes’ conditional probabilities and applied an exact binomial test to perform reverse inference. Both datasets showed robust post-eruption cooling signals, the strongest being within t0 +3 years. Precipitation responses were controversial: REACHES revealed overall wetting, whereas ModE-RA suggested drying, indicating a consistent cooling effect of major volcanic eruptions and divergent responses in hydroclimates. Future analysis should focus on the hydroclimatic effects of volcanic eruptions using high-resolution reconstruction data and simulations.

title: Differentiating Westerly and Asian monsoon dust fluxes to the tropical Pacific Ocean since the late Pliocene
abstract: Asian dust flux is a fundamental regulator of global climate and marine biogeochemical cycles, yet it is difficult to separate the dust fractions delivered to the tropical Pacific Ocean by the Westerlies and East Asian Winter Monsoon (EAWM). We present a 4-million-year record of eolian evolution from the Philippine Sea to deconvolve these two distinct transport systems on the basis of grain-size modeling and geochemical fingerprinting. Our results show that the Westerlies component is primarily derived from hyper-arid deserts, whereas the EAWM-driven component originates from the semi-arid margins of East and Central Asia. Of importance is the finding that Westerly-driven transport reflects a coherent response to global cooling and hemispheric thermal gradients, whilst the Asia monsoon contribution is mediated by vegetation cover. We further demonstrate that hydroclimatic fluctuations in EAWM marginal zones modulate dust availability through vegetation-induced surface roughness and pedogenic refinement, resulting in a pronounced non-linear relationship between dust flux and wind energetics. This suggests the ecological conditions of dust source regions exert an impact on dust flux and thus the tropical ocean, necessitating integration of dynamic vegetation impacts and anthropogenic landscape interventions on dust into Earth System Models to predict global carbon cycling in a warming world. “Ecological conditions of dust source regions exert an impact on dust flux and thus on the tropical ocean, shown using grain size modeling and geochemical fingerprinting of a 4-million-year-long sediment record from the Philippine Sea”

title: 4D sensitivity kernels for infrasound atmospheric propagation: considering the need and impact of time dependent observation operators for acoustic wave observations in data assimilation methods
abstract: arXiv:2610.36810v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The long range propagation of acoustic waves in Earth's atmosphere is sensitive to winds and temperature variations in the upper atmosphere. Thus, infrasound observations have a strong potential to improve numerical weather models by data assimilation methods. However, because acoustic waves propagate slowly, the atmospheric parameters can change during the propagation of the acoustic waves. This change of atmosphere properties is usually not taken into account by infrasound simulation tools which generally assume stationary atmosphere models. In order to close this modeling gap, we present here a method to compute the linear sensitivities of infrasound observables to atmospheric parameters varying both in space and time. We show that adjoint based methods can easily handle this computation of 4D sensitivity kernels, also called time variable observation operators in the data assimilation community. Then, we discuss the capabilities of various data assimilation methods to handle such observation operators. We demonstrate that only variational methods with data assimilation windows longer than the propagation duration of the long range infrasound can accommodate these observations, as well as their ensemble counterparts. Finally, we demonstrate the benefit of assimilating such long range infrasound observations, and we quantify the relative impact of linear approximation of observation operators and stationary approximation of the atmosphere model by assimilating propagation time observations of circumnavigating Lamb waves in Lorenz'96 low-order model. The results of this data assimilation experiment demonstrate that the time variability of atmospheric parameters should be taken into account even for infrasound propagation times limited to 2 or 3 time steps of the atmosphere model.

title: Geochemical and granulometric fingerprints of 8200 years of westerly wind variability in inner‐fjord lake sediments from Svalbard
abstract: The Arctic is warming faster than any other region on Earth. As sea ice diminishes, the surface boundary conditions, such as roughness and air–sea coupling, change and open‐water fetch increases. This may enhance wind forcing on Arctic coasts. Lake sediments can record these changes through the deposition of wind‐blown grains and elements, offering insights into past wind and climate dynamics. We reconstruct c . 8200 years of wind and climate variability using laminated sediments from a closed‐basin lake in central Spitsbergen, Svalbard archipelago, High Arctic. By integrating geochemical, visual and granulometric fingerprints within a multiproxy geostatistical framework, we link aeolian minerogenic input to specific catchment sources. Our findings show that iron (Fe)‐rich coarse silt‐sized clasts originate from distinct dolerite outcrops west and northwest of the lake, upwind of the dominant summer westerlies. This reveals a locally filtered westerly input that aligns with valley‐fjord channelling. We identify four phases of enhanced aeolian activity during the Mid‐ and Late Holocene, which occurred when local boundary conditions were favourable for entraining and transporting sediment into the basin. Major shifts in sediment sources and depositional conditions coincide with the end of the Holocene Thermal Maximum and the gradual onset of the Neoglacial. However, the reconstructed wind signal demonstrates a comparatively stable long‐term behaviour, with no clear correspondence to regional palaeoclimate records.

title: Contrasting Tropical SST Warming in Two Climate Models: The Roles of Winds, Clouds, Evaporative Cooling, and Ocean Dynamics
abstract: Abstract To investigate why climate models simulate diverse tropical Pacific sea surface temperature (SST) changes under greenhouse-gas forcing, we utilize two configurations of the Community Earth System Model (CESM2) that differ in their atmospheric component (CAM6 and CAM4). Under abrupt CO 2 quadrupling, CAM6 simulates over double the weakening of the east-west equatorial SST gradient compared to CAM4 by end-of-century. To understand this contrast, we conduct overriding experiments that replace wind stress, or wind stress and shortwave fluxes, with values from the preindustrial control experiment. In CAM6, low clouds amplify climate warming and act as a forcing and positive feedback on reductions in the east-west SST gradient. In contrast, in CAM4, low clouds act as a negative climate feedback and provide little contribution to the SST gradient reduction. In both models, interactive wind stress leads to a strong positive feedback (i.e., the Bjerknes feedback). The two models also diverge in their short-term SST responses: CAM6 exhibits an immediate weakening of the zonal SST gradient, while CAM4 initially shows a steepening. Our findings highlight the importance of shortwave radiative and Bjerknes feedbacks, evaporative cooling, and ocean dynamics, all of which control tropical Pacific SST pattern formation.

title: 40-kyr of environmental history of the southeastern sector of paleolake Cuitzeo, central-western Mexico: Insights from abiotic and biotic proxies
abstract: We present a multiproxy reconstruction of environmental changes recorded in the southeastern sector of Lake Cuitzeo (central-western Mexico) over the last ∼40 kyr. Our study integrates abiotic (major-element geochemistry, rock-magnetic parameters, pH, and electrical conductivity) and biotic proxies (diatoms and pollen) from a ∼10 m-long sedimentary core (Cz-07). This multiproxy approach provides a robust framework for identifying variations in terrigenous input, redox conditions, nutrient availability, carbonate precipitation, and hydrological balance, as well as the response of local vegetation to climate fluctuations. Comparing the Cz-07 record with previous data from a depocenter core reveals some spatial differences in the lake’s sensitivity to environmental changes. The sequence indicates generally low lake levels between ∼42 and ∼26.5 kyr BP, followed by pronounced environmental variability during the Last Glacial Maximum, including a marked dry episode at its onset. Enhanced runoff and predominantly oxic conditions characterize the interval from ∼17.5 to ∼11 kyr BP, encompassing the Bølling–Allerød and Younger Dryas events. During the early-to-middle Holocene (∼11.7–5 kyr BP), a progressive shift toward arid conditions is evidenced by increased carbonate precipitation, higher salinity, and reduced runoff. The most severe drought occurred during the middle Holocene, causing a substantial contraction of the lake’s southeastern sector. This arid phase aligns with middle Holocene drying trends reported in other lacustrine records across central Mexico.

title: Diversity of South China Sea Marine Heatwave Intensity Trends
abstract: Abstract This study investigates the seasonal characteristics and physical drivers of marine heatwave (MHW) intensity trends in the South China Sea (SCS) during 1993–2022. Results reveal a robust, seasonally consistent north-south divergent pattern: MHW intensity has intensified pronouncedly in the northern and northwestern SCS while declining on decadal timescales in the southwestern basin, forming a "rich-get-richer, poor-get-poorer" contrast. Mixed-layer heat budget diagnostics show that enhanced net surface heat flux (Qnet), driven by increased shortwave radiation (SSR) and reduced latent heat loss, primarily causes MHW intensification in the northern and northwestern SCS. In contrast, changes in the South China Sea West Boundary Current (SCS WBC) dominate in the southwestern SCS, where a weakening northward WBC in summer and strengthening southward WBC in winter shift horizontal advection toward net cooling, and thereby weakens MHWs. Teleconnection analyses link this regional disparity to different large-scale climate modes across seasons. Strengthening of the Indian Ocean Dipole (IOD) and Atlantic Multidecadal Oscillation (AMO) respectively increase SSR over the northern SCS during summer and winter, while the negative phase shift of the Pacific Decadal Oscillation (PDO) and ENSO weakens anticyclonic forcing that modulates the SCS WBC in the southwestern SCS in both seasons. These findings highlight the importance of seasonal and regional heterogeneity in MHW dynamics for improving the prediction of extreme ocean warming in marginal seas.

title: Late-glacial and Holocene vegetation dynamics in response to climate, land use and fire at Lago di Andromia (Ossola, Italian Alps)
abstract: Understanding of past vegetation dynamics provides valuable information to better assess future ecosystem impacts under global change. In this context, the European Alps offer the opportunity to study diverse environments. Here, we present a multi-proxy palaeoecological study from the Pennine Alps combining pollen, spores, stomata, charcoal and plant macrofossil analysis. We reconstructed the vegetation dynamics over the past ca. 14,000 years based on sediment cores from Lago di Andromia (1926 m a.s.l.), a small lake located in the subalpine belt of the Ossola valley (Italy). During the Allerød the site was just above the treeline, before Larix decidua trees reached it ca. 11,500 years ago, in response to Holocene warming. Pinus cembra established locally ca. 500 years later, whereas Abies alba reached the site at the latest ca. 10,500 years ago and became co-dominant after 10,000 cal yr BP . Our new evidence confirms that the Ossola valley was an important corridor for the spread of Abies alba across the Alps, highlighting the crucial role of mid-to high elevations for its Holocene range expansion. Vegetation structure and composition remained rather stable during the Holocene Thermal Maximum (ca. 10,000–5000 cal yr BP). Earliest evidence for local pastoralism dates to 5500 years ago and was linked to anthropogenic fires to clear forests. During the Early Bronze Age (ca. 4200 years ago), both pastoral and arable farming increased in the valley, leading to a marked opening in the vegetation. Although sparse, evidence of Juglans regia cultivation during the Late-Neolithic coincides with similar results in Northern Italy, suggesting a striking centrality of the Andromia area, likely tied to its position at the confluence of five Alpine valleys close to the present-day city of Domodossola.

title: Deploying machine learning components coupled to Earth  System Models with OASIS3-MCT (v6) and Eophis (v1.1)
abstract: Scientists use programs, called Earth System Models, to study and predict climate. These models are based on physical theories but can be completed with AI tools. However, combining these tools with traditional models is difficult due to their different nature. Our research introduces a new method that connects these AI tools with existing climate models. We tested this method by integrating it with an ocean model. This work should help scientists explore new ways of making climate predictions.

title: A Basin‐Wise GLOF Susceptibility Assessment in the Western Himalayas: Integrating Remote Sensing‐ GIS and Multi‐Criteria Decision Analysis
abstract: ABSTRACT Glacial Lake Outburst Floods (GLOFs) pose an increasing threat to high mountain environments across the world, especially in the Himalayas where climate change is accelerating glacier retreat and permafrost degradation. This study presents a detailed GLOF susceptibility analysis of the western Himalayas covering five major river basins, ie Satluj, Chenab, Jhelum, Beas, and Ravi by integrating high‐resolution remote sensing data with a multi‐criteria decision‐making approach. A detailed inventory of 1573 glacial lakes was developed using manual delineation of Sentinel‐2A and LISS‐IV images. Forty‐eight potentially dangerous lakes were identified based on size and dam composition. Following the guidelines of NDMA and GAPHAZ, 12 important physical and geomorphic parameters were selected and evaluated using Analytic Hierarchy Process (AHP) with the addition of Cumulative Weightage Technique (CWT). AHP Analysis indicated that 20 lakes were high hazard, 23 lakes were medium hazard, and five lakes were low hazard. The basin‐wise analysis revealed that Satluj and Chenab are particularly vulnerable owing to the presence of large and fast‐growing lakes. A temporal assessment of 48 selected potentially dangerous lakes from 2000 to 2024 revealed a 115% increase in total lake area, highlighting their rapid expansion under a warming climate. The susceptibility framework was validated using seven historical GLOF events, all of which had hazard scores > 0.7, in agreement with the high susceptibility lakes identified in this study. The study recommends that detailed field investigations be carried out on high‐hazard lakes including bathymetric surveys, assessments of moraine stability, and real‐time monitoring to validate remote sensing findings and to inform early warning systems. This approach offers a transferable and policy‐relevant framework to support GLOF risk mitigation and climate adaptation planning in glacierized regions. This study relies primarily on remote sensing data, and uncertainties in lake identification and the lack of field validation may affect susceptibility classification.

title: Evolution of the Tibetan Plateau-Northern Indian Ocean thermal contrast since the last deglaciation and its regulation of the Indian Summer Monsoon
High- and low-latitude forcing on precipitation variations over the central Qilian Mountains since 18.5 ka
abstract: The moisture of the northeastern Tibetan Plateau is jointly shaped by the East Asian Summer Monsoon (EASM) and the mid-latitude Westerlies, the two key atmospheric circulation systems originating from low- and high-latitudes, respectively. Modern observations demonstrate that the intensity change and meridional position of the Westerlies directly modulate the EASM precipitation, which sustains vast human populations and ecosystems across East Asia. However, the interaction between these two systems over geological time remains controversial, partly due to controversies in the reconstructed past precipitation intensity. Here, we present a high-resolution multi-proxy loess record (ZES) spanning the past 18.5 ka from the central Qilian Mountains, located in the monsoon marginal zone where both systems jointly operate. We first found that loess–paleosol carbonate δ 18 O of ZES record captures a summer signal and covaries inversely with δ 13 C, which tracks monsoon precipitation intensity. Together with comparisons between modern observations and geological records, this constrains EASM-dominated precipitation. We then establish a robust EASM index from multiple independent proxies including magnetic susceptibility, total carbonate content, dolomite content, carbonate δ 13 C, and colour reflectance. Our results reveal that EASM precipitation responded to combined high- and low-latitude forcing on both millennial timescales during the Last Deglaciation and orbital timescales manifested in the long-term trend since 18.5 ka, with the pre-Boreal oscillation offering complementary insights into early-Holocene centennial-scale interactions. The EASM precipitation intensity was suppressed during the Last Deglaciation, strengthened gradually through the early Holocene, peaked from ∼7.5 to 1.8 ka, and subsequently declined. Direct comparison of Westerlies and EASM signals retrieved from the same loess sequence reveals coupled interaction between the two systems since the mid-late Holocene, with westerly intensification accompanying monsoon strengthening. These findings indicate bidirectional linkage between high- and low-latitude systems and further suggest that, under continued global warming, the monsoon marginal zone of northwestern China may experience a progressive increase in precipitation.

abstract: arXiv:2610.36297v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Coupled climate simulations are computationally expensive, largely because of the atmosphere. We introduce FASST, a coupled climate model that retains the prognostic POP2 ocean while replacing the atmosphere and sea ice with lightweight U-Net emulators. The atmospheric emulator is diagnostic, predicting surface fluxes from the evolving ocean-ice state every $6$ simulated hours, while the sea-ice emulator advances the ice state monthly. For $140$ years of unforced integration, FASST maintains a stable global-mean climate without SST restoring, with post-transient global-mean SST of $291.30 \pm 0.22\mathrm{K}$ compared with $291.25 \pm 0.10\mathrm{K}$ in CESM$2$ piControl. FASST also captures interannual Ni\~no-$3.4$ variability, although with weaker amplitude than CESM ($0.62\mathrm{K}$ versus $1.02\mathrm{K}$). These results demonstrate that a stateless learned atmosphere can sustain stable, free-running coupled climate simulations over century-scale integrations.

title: Impact of Cumulus Parameterization and Cloud Microphysics on WRF Simulation of an Extreme Rainfall Event over Maharashtra, India: A 3 by 3 Factorial Assessment
abstract: arXiv:2610.36944v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Simulating extreme monsoon rainfall over the Konkan coast and Western Ghats remains challenging at 9 km resolution, where convection is partly resolved and partly parameterised. This study evaluates the sensitivity of Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) simulations of the 5-7 July 2026 Maharashtra rainfall event to cumulus and cloud microphysics schemes. Nine simulations employed a 3 x 3 factorial design combining WSM6, WDM6 and Thompson microphysics with Kain-Fritsch, Tiedtke and Grell-Freitas cumulus schemes. Rainfall was evaluated against IMD 0.25-degree gridded observations, with IMERG and ERA5 as additional references. A descriptive factorial decomposition showed that cumulus parameterisation accounted for 97.3% of across-experiment variation in mean rainfall, 88.2% in RMSE and 84.7% in spatial correlation, while microphysics contributed 2.0%, 2.1% and 9.3%, respectively. Kain-Fritsch produced the highest spatial correlations (0.533-0.581) but substantially overestimated rainfall. Tiedtke achieved the smallest mean biases and RMSE, although compensating regional errors concealed a 28-34% rainfall deficit over the Konkan-Ghats belt and substantial underestimation on 7 July. Grell-Freitas showed large wet biases and relatively high RMSE. All nine simulations displaced the event-total rainfall maximum approximately 140-195 km northward. WSM6-Tiedtke achieved the lowest RMSE, whereas Thompson-Kain-Fritsch better represented the rainfall spatial pattern. The findings demonstrate that, for this event and fixed model configuration, cumulus parameterisation exerted substantially greater influence on simulated rainfall than cloud microphysics. However, a single-event, single-member experimental design does not establish a universally optimal physics configuration.

title: Regional climatic change following the Eocene–Oligocene Transition in central northern Tibet
abstract: The Eocene–Oligocene Transition (EOT) constitutes one of the most dramatic climatic changes in the Cenozoic era; it is characterized by global cooling, increasing aridity, extinction of fauna and flora, and a major drop of global sea level. However, how continental settings responded to global climatic change after the EOT event has still received little consideration. Here we report a high-resolution and well-dated terrestrial EOT record from the Tuotuohe Basin (central northern Tibetan Plateau). Sedimentary facies, fossil evidence, new proxy, and climate modeling data suggest a transition from warm and dry to cool and wet climatic conditions ca. 33 Ma, in contrast with other records from the Tibetan Plateau that commonly document drier conditions after the EOT (ca. 34 Ma). Having considered the potential forcing mechanisms, we propose that the Indian monsoon likely expanded into the Tuotuohe Basin after the EOT due to a combination of factors, such as the land-sea pressure gradient caused by the retreat of the Paratethys Sea, tectonic uplift in central northern Tibet and increased cross-equatorial pressure gradients. This study opens new perspectives for paleoclimate model simulations around the EOT that encompasses major environmental reorganizations at the continent scale, such as the Mongolian Re-modeling (faunal turnovers of Paleogene mammals from the Mongolian Plateau) and the Grande Coupure (extinction of a large number of European native mammals).
