abstract: by Elyas Hannoufa, Eric Johlin Building-integrated photovoltaics (BIPV) are a promising strategy for enhancing building energy performance and reducing carbon emissions. However, most design optimization studies rely on historical climate datasets that may fail to capture the operating conditions buildings will experience under climate change. This study develops a computational framework for the multi-objective optimization of BIPV envelope systems using future climate projections from the CanESM5 model under the SSP3-7.0 scenario. We analyze two system configurations, awning shades and thin-film window coatings, across four cities with diverse climates (Berlin, Los Angeles, Chicago, Singapore), comparing results from conventional EPW files, NASA 2023 historical data, and 2046–2050 climate scenarios. Optimization integrates electricity generation, thermal loads, and daylighting quality to capture building-level trade-offs. Results show that traditional EPW datasets systematically under-predict BIPV performance, particularly in Berlin and Los Angeles. Under 2046–2050 projected conditions, all four cities exhibit performance gains: substantial in Berlin, Chicago and Los Angeles, and marginal in Singapore, with the largest absolute gains in Los Angeles. By 2050, unshaded windows transition to consistently detrimental for building energy balance. Thin-film coatings achieve optimal outcomes at high absorptance, in the 80–90% range, contrary to current low-absorption design practice. Within the CanESM5 SSP3-7.0 scenario examined, these findings show that projected climate conditions can substantially reshape the modeled performance landscape of BIPV systems, emphasizing the need for forward-looking climate projections in building design optimization and the growing importance of BIPV for climate-adaptive and resilient urban buildings.

title: BorFIT: a novel LiDAR-based training dataset  for individual tree segmentation and species  detection in northern boreal forests
abstract: BorFIT is a novel training dataset for light detection and ranging (LiDAR) point cloud segmentation and tree species detection in boreal forests. Comprising 384 plots across Siberia, Canada, and Alaska, it features 16 530 manually segmented trees of 12 species. BorFIT supports artificial intelligence (AI) applications for analyzing species distribution, stand structure, and boreal forest response to climate change.

title: Linking rain-on-snow events to river floods in the Tianshan Mountains
abstract: Rain-on-snow (ROS) events are widely recognized as an important cryosphere–hydrology coupling mechanism, yet when and where ROS events translate into river floods remains poorly constrained, particularly in arid high-mountain regions. Here, we provide the first basin-scale assessment of potential flood-inducing ROS (ROS-PF) and actual river-flood-generating ROS (ROS-AF) events across the Tianshan Mountains. Using ERA5-Land reanalysis (1951–2019) and an observation-based reconstructed daily streamflow dataset covering 40 Tianshan watersheds, we link ROS forcing to reconstructed high-flow responses. ROS-PF events—defined by rainfall ≥10 mm occurring on snowpack with snow water equivalent ≥10 mm—are concentrated in spring (April–June) and mid-elevations (2.0–3.5 km), within a narrow temperature window of–0.24 ± 1.49 °C. Their frequency has increased significantly over the past seven decades, driven primarily by rising heavy rainfall occurrence rather than snow availability. On average, ROS-PF events contributed on average 14.7% of the 6-day snowmelt total and 8.3% of the 6-day available-water total across the Tianshan basins. Crucially, only ∼44% of ROS-PF events evolve into ROS-AF events, revealing strong basin-dependent conversion efficiency. Some basins like Pochengzi basin convert nearly all ROS-PF events into floods, while others exhibit high ROS-PF frequency but minimal flood response. Most ROS-AF events occur with a lag of up to six days, underscoring the importance of delayed hydrological responses. These findings demonstrate that ROS does not uniformly amplify flood risk but instead reorganizes flood-generation pathways under warming, with implications for flood forecasting and water management in arid mountain systems.

title: Using a two-stage Rosenbrock solver to increase computational efficiency in the DOE's Exascale Earth   System Model version 1 (E3SMv1)
abstract: We implemented a two-stage Rosenbrock solver (ROS2) in E3SMv1 and evaluated it with two atmospheric chemistry mechanisms. At a 180 s timestep, ROS2 reduced chemistry integration time by ~33% versus the original implicit solver on Cori/KNL CPUs, while maintaining stable one-year simulations and small ozone differences (≤1.03 ppb). Species-dependent differences in ozone, NO, NO2, and OH were small. Results support ROS2 as a lower-cost option, with further convergence and CPU/GPU testing needed.

title: Technical note: Evaluation of snow water equivalent from large-scale land-surface products over Italy
abstract: Abstract. Snow water equivalent (SWE) is a critical hydrological variable for water resource management in mountainous regions, where seasonal snowpacks function as natural reservoirs regulating streamflow and water supply. While high-resolution, observation-constrained regional or national snow products provide reliable daily SWE estimates at fine spatial resolution (less than 1 km), their limited temporal coverage often restricts their use for long-term hydro-climatological studies. Large-scale land-surface products, in which SWE is derived from land-surface model simulations driven by atmospheric reanalyses or regional dynamical downscaling systems, provide multi-decadal coverage, but their reliability may be affected by biases in meteorological forcing, limited topographic representation, and simplified snow process parameterisation, requiring rigorous regional evaluation. This study evaluates the SWE estimates of three large-scale land-surface products, i.e., the global ERA5-Land, the European CERRA-Land, and the Italian VHR-REA_IT, against the national reference dataset IT-SNOW across Italy. The analysis combines grid-scale bias assessment of mean annual SWE and snow cover duration with temporal correlation analysis of daily SWE series, and is complemented by an evaluation of precipitation and temperature biases in each product, providing insight into how each product represents the atmospheric conditions governing snow accumulation and ablation and thereby supporting the interpretation of the identified SWE discrepancies. The results show clear regional differences in product performance, with no single product performing best across all metrics. ERA5-Land shows the strongest temporal correlation with IT-SNOW, but tends to overestimate mean annual SWE and snow cover duration in the Alps. CERRA-Land shows more moderate biases than ERA5-Land in the Italian Alps, but generally underestimates mean annual SWE across most subregions, where autumn and winter precipitation deficits in the forcing limit snow accumulation. Across the Apennines, both ERA5-Land and CERRA-Land tend to underestimate SWE and snow cover duration, particularly in the northern sectors. VHR-REA_IT shows widespread underestimation and the weakest temporal correspondence with IT-SNOW: this may be due to its fully coupled atmosphere–land architecture with no assimilation of meteorological observations. Overall, the results suggest that forcing biases explain a substantial part of the observed SWE discrepancies, although not all of them. This study provides useful insights for the use of SWE estimates from large-scale land-surface products in long-term hydro-climatological assessments over Italy and helps to understand whether the products can be used to evaluate snow dynamics in mountainous regions lacking high-quality benchmark estimates.

title: Towards operational data-driven regional weather forecasting: extreme-event skill and near-real-time verification with HRRRCast
abstract: arXiv:2610.36186v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Improving convective-scale skill in data-driven regional weather models requires better representing rare high-impact events, training at native resolution, broadening variable output, and demonstrating performance in real-time settings. Here, we evaluate these challenges using HRRRCast, a data-driven convection-allowing emulator trained on the High-Resolution Rapid Refresh (HRRR) analysis data. HRRRCast combines native 3-km training, moderate sigmoid-weighted loss reweighting for reflectivity and precipitation, and broader system improvements including expansion of the training archive from 3 to 9 years (2016--2025), increased vertical resolution, expanded outputs, and architectural upgrades. The weighted loss improves high-threshold skill while preserving common-event behavior. Native-resolution training avoids aliasing from 6-km subsampling and substantially improves fractions skill score at convective scales, with gains that persist across pooling windows. HRRRCast has also been running in near-real-time mode for the past year. In seven months of independent observation-based verification, HRRRCast ensemble means improve several near-surface metrics relative to operational HRRR and maintain strong precipitation and reflectivity performance. Single-member reflectivity skill is strongest at 20--30 dBZ; at 40 dBZ, skill is near parity at 6-km pooling and better at pooling radii $\geq$30 km. Precipitation skill remains competitive through 1 in/h and extends to about 3 in/h in the best recent configuration. A focused comparison with HREF further shows useful low-cost probabilistic guidance for 3-h precipitation. At storm scale, HRRRCast exhibits a displacement--structure trade-off, with generally better storm placement than storm morphology.

title: Reconstruction of the 1989 Laguna del Cerro Largo GLOF: an interdisciplinary understanding of GLOF Impacts
journal: Natural hazards and earth system sciences
abstract: Abstract. The March 16, 1989, glacial lake outburst flood (GLOF) from Laguna del Cerro Largo in Valle Soler, Aysén, Chile, is one of the largest recent moraine-dammed GLOFs in the region. This interdisciplinary approach reconstructs the GLOF downstream impacts using HEC-RAS 2D and GeoClaw from witness accounts. Model results are then validated through field analysis of sediment deposition, dendrogeomorphic surveys, radiocarbon dating. Sediment cores reveal distinct clastic layers attributable to the 1989 event and evidence of an earlier outburst flood from the adjacent Laguna Turbio, dated circa 125 ybp. The model results also indicate a substantially higher peak discharge than official reports, impacting subsequent disaster policy decades later. While dendrogeomorphic sampling was hindered by fungal decay in Nothofagus species, the findings highlight both the potential and limitations of interdisciplinary reconstructions of GLOF events in remote, data-scarce environments.

title: Prediction-Constrained Multimodal Temporal Fusion of Satellite Microwave and Infrared Observations for Continuous Snow Temperature Profile Estimation
abstract: Snow temperature profiles are important for characterizing snowpack thermal state and vertical heat transfer, but continuous estimation is limited by sparse in situ observations and discrete satellite overpasses. This study proposes a prediction-constrained multimodal temporal fusion method combining continuous deep-learning prediction with satellite microwave–infrared updates. The Weather-Forced Residual LSTM with Persistence Fallback (WFRL-P) generates an hourly multi-depth prediction background from historical snow temperatures and meteorological forcing. Snow temperature profiles are then conjointly retrieved from AMSR2 microwave and MODIS infrared brightness temperatures, and valid retrieval–prediction differences are transformed into depth-dependent, magnitude-limited updates and causally propagated for up to 6 h. Independent evaluation at Dome C during 2020–2021 produced hourly estimates at 12 depths from 5 to 1000 cm, with an all-depth bias of −0.1263 K, MAE of 0.3657 K, RMSE of 0.8218 K, and R2 of 0.9880. At most comparable depths, the estimation errors were lower than those reported in previous Antarctic snow temperature remote-sensing studies. Multimodal fusion further reduced the all-depth MAE of the fixed lead-24 prediction background by 3.32%, with a 5.14% improvement at matched satellite-overpass samples. The results demonstrate that satellite microwave and infrared observations can provide effective incremental constraints while maintaining the overall accuracy of the continuous prediction background, offering a feasible approach for the temporal fusion of discrete satellite observations and continuous snow temperature predictions.

title: Snow and Ice Cover Change in the Earth's Third Pole: Implications for Future Water Resources
abstract: The Tibetan Plateau, Earth's "Third Pole," holds critical glacial water reserves that sustain billions of people across Asia. Climate change drives widespread glacier retreat across the region, but melt rates vary sharply by location, creating a need for fine-scale local monitoring to support adaptive water management. This study quantifies annual late-summer changes in snow and ice cover in a 100 × 125 mile central Himalayan study area near Mount Everest, using Landsat 8 satellite imagery processed in Google Earth Engine with the Normalized Difference Snow Index. Year-to-year changes were measured via image subtraction for 13 intervals from 2013 to 2026, and linear regression with a t-test was used to evaluate long-term trends. Results show net annual snow and ice loss across all 13 year-to-year intervals, although the magnitude of loss varies widely from year to year. A slight negative trend in annual loss was not statistically significant (p = 0.458), indicating no clear statistically significant long-term change in the annual loss trend over the study period. These local findings complement regional assessments and support targeted water resource planning for communities dependent on Third Pole meltwater.

title: Hydroclimate Variability at Lake Tana, Ethiopia, Over the Past 6,000 Years: A Critical Synthesis of Geochemical and Isotopic Records
abstract: Lake Tana, the source of the Blue Nile in the northwestern Ethiopian highlands, is a climatically sensitive archive at the northern margin of the Intertropical Convergence Zone (ITCZ). Its sediments record changes in the balance between Atlantic/Congo Basin moisture and Indian Ocean/Red Sea moisture, making it a key site for understanding Afro-Asian monsoon dynamics. This review critically synthesizes geochemical (XRF element ratios: Zr/Rb, Ca/Ti, Rb/K) and isotopic (leaf-wax δD) records from Lake Tana to reconstruct hydroclimate variability over the past 6,000 years, evaluate proxy reliability, and identify research gaps. Available evidence indicates that the African Humid Period (AHP) terminated at Lake Tana by approximately 8,000 cal BP, significantly earlier than in the Sahara and North Africa (~5,000 cal BP), δDwax records indicate that this transition was driven by eastward migration of the Congo Air Boundary (CAB), not solely by ITCZ southward retreat. Late Holocene aridification culminated in a pronounced low-stand at ~4,200 cal BP, coeval with the Egyptian Old Kingdom collapse. Existing XRF data (366–150,190 yr) provide a foundation but lack the sampling density needed to resolve centennial-scale variability in the past 6,000 years, and no dedicated high-resolution study exists for the past 2,000 years, a period encompassing the Aksumite civilization and the Little Ice Age. A dedicated high-resolution geochemical and isotopic study is urgently needed to address outstanding questions about natural variability versus anthropogenic impact, and to provide a longer historical context for water resource management in the Blue Nile basin under future global warming.

title: Ice breakup dynamics on the Kuskokwim River: climatic trends and hydro-meteorological drivers
abstract: River ice breakup is a critical hydrological process governing flood risk and transportation in sub-arctic regions. This study investigates hydroclimatic drivers of breakup timing on the lower Kuskokwim River, Alaska, synthesizing a 102-year observational record (1924–2025) with ERA5 reanalysis. Statistical analysis reveals a winter warming trend driving a phenological advancement of 0.77 days per decade, yet inter-decadal timing variance remains persistently high. Classifying historical events into early, normal, and late categories demonstrate that despite varying spring warming rates, the ice cover consistently requires ∼ 231°C-days of thermal accumulation to reach structural susceptibility. Late breakups are delayed by deep spring snowpacks acting as thermal insulators, not by differing thermal requirements. While atmospheric heat pre-conditions the ice, pre-breakup discharge acts as an independent mechanical trigger. These results provide a categorical framework for tracking warming trajectories and contextualizing extreme events in data-limited basins.

title: Monsoon zonal seesaw: Development of the South Asian monsoon aridified North Africa in the Cenozoic
abstract: North Africa experienced a pronounced transition from humid to arid conditions during the early Cenozoic. Meanwhile, the South Asian monsoon underwent substantial intensification, largely driven by the uplift of the Himalayan-Tibetan Plateau. Here, we demonstrate that the two events, which greatly shaped the paleoenvironment and modern regional climate, are not independent responses to paleogeography changes; rather, the former is primarily driven by the latter through the monsoon-desert mechanism, in which South Asian monsoon diabatic heating produces large-scale subsidence and aridity over North Africa. Using multiple ensembles of paleoclimate simulations and a model for the atmospheric response to imposed diabatic heating, we show that the intensification and poleward shift of Asian monsoon rainfall each make comparable contributions to the aridification of North Africa. Our findings identify a persistent dynamical pathway linking the South Asian and North African monsoons and suggest that it played a major role in early Cenozoic North African aridification, while its climatic expression at other times depended on the relative strengths of competing forcings.

title: MLAWind: a monthly sea surface wind dataset derived from an interpretable machine learning approach integrating in-situ observations and satellite data
abstract: This study develops a monthly near-global sea surface wind dataset (MLAWind) from 1950–2023 through an interpretable machine learning framework integrating in-situ observations and satellite data. Evaluations show that MLAWind achieves comparable performance to the widely-used reanalysis datasets at different time scales. It provides reliable historical wind data during both satellite and non-satellite periods, demonstrating broad application prospects in ocean and climate research.

title: SATFRONT: Detecting Atmospheric Fronts with Satellite Data using Machine Learning
abstract: arXiv:2610.42111v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Atmospheric fronts are associated with much of the high-impact weather in the mid-latitudes, yet their identification and classification remain largely manual and subjective. Existing deep learning approaches rely primarily on gridded reanalysis or forecast data, limiting their applicability to satellite observations available for time-critical applications. We introduce SATFRONT, a machine learning framework for detecting cold, warm, and occluded fronts over Europe from geostationary satellite observations, with reanalysis data as an optional additional input. The model is trained on frontal analyses from five European national meteorological services and evaluated against UK Met Office analyses for 2024. Using satellite observations alone, SATFRONT achieves a Critical Success Index (CSI) of 0.428 at a 150 km tolerance, within the range of agreement between analyses from different meteorological services (0.277-0.501) and higher than that of an operational rule-based front detector that uses satellite data (0.133). Adding ERA5 reanalysis increases the CSI to 0.591. ERA5 substantially improves the placement of individual fronts, although its effect on their annual spatial distribution varies by front type. These results demonstrate that cold, warm, and occluded fronts can be detected directly from geostationary satellite observations, providing a basis for automated frontal analyses at the high temporal frequency required for time-critical applications.

title: Machine Learning Sensor Fusion for Water Vapor Radiometry based Tropospheric Delay Calibration
abstract: arXiv:2610.41052v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The next-generation Very Large Array (ngVLA) intends to use 22 GHz water vapor radiometry (WVR) to correct for tropospheric phase fluctuations in its high-frequency bands. However, current delay-retrieval methods do not reach the required accuracy and reliability. As a remedy, we propose a machine-learning based retrieval concept and a preliminary architecture, framed as heterogeneous, multi-rate sensor fusion. Atmospheric reanalysis profiles and surface weather set the context in which per-antenna WVR spectra are used to estimate excess path by a Kalman filter whose parameters are learned from high-cadence calibrator phases. The method is being developed, with planned first validation on the 183 GHz WVR system of the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA).

title: On combining climate models into weighted ensembles
abstract: We provide practical guidelines for producing weighted ensembles of climate models. We distinguish between two approaches, the individual- and the ensemble performance weighting approach, and formulate both in probabilistic terms, making the underlying assumptions transparent. Using constructed examples, we show the advantage of the ensemble weighting approach to account for model co-dependencies and examine how methodological choices affect the climate projections of the weighted ensemble.

title: MioOcean: database compilation and temperature proxy systematics in the Miocene oceans
abstract: Preprint under review for ESSD (discussion: open, 0 comments) The MioOcean database hosts Miocene (23–5.3 million years ago) ocean temperatures, standardised and with updated age information, comprising 22,941 data points from 101 scientific studies. As parts of the Miocene were warmer than present, with estimated CO2 levels similar to those projected for the near future, this database enables assessment of how past oceans responded to climate variations, which may improve predictions of climate responses to anticipated future warming.

title: Ensemble-size-dependence of deep-learning post-processing methods that minimize an (un)fair score: motivating examples and a proof-of-concept solution
abstract: arXiv:2602.15830v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Fair scores reward ensemble forecast members that behave like samples from the same distribution as the verifying observations. They are therefore an attractive choice as loss functions to train data-driven ensemble forecasts or post-processing methods when large training ensembles are either unavailable or computationally prohibitive. The adjusted continuous ranked probability score (aCRPS) is a fair and ensemble-size-unbiased scoring rule when applied to ensembles with forecast members that are interpretable as conditionally independent draws from an underlying predictive distribution. However, distribution-aware post-processing methods that introduce structural dependency between members can violate this assumption, such that aCRPS no longer functions as a fair scoring rule. We demonstrate this effect using two approaches designed to minimize the expected aCRPS of a finite ensemble: (1) a linear member-by-member calibration, which couples members through a common dependency on the sample ensemble mean, and (2) a deep-learning method, which couples members via transformer self-attention across the ensemble dimension. In both cases, the results are sensitive to ensemble size and apparent gains in aCRPS can correspond to systematic unreliability characterized by over-dispersion. We introduce trajectory transformers as a proof-of-concept that ensemble-size independence can be achieved. This approach is an adaptation of the Post-processing Ensembles with Transformers (PoET) framework and applies self-attention over lead time while preserving the conditional independence required by aCRPS. When applied to weekly mean $T_{2m}$ forecasts from the ECMWF subseasonal forecasting system, this approach successfully reduces systematic model biases whilst also improving or maintaining forecast reliability regardless of the ensemble size used in training or real-time forecasts.

title: A Comparative Study of Convolutional and Recurrent Neural Networks for Storm Surge Prediction in Tampa Bay
abstract: arXiv:2408.05797v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: In this paper, we compare the performance of three popular deep learning architectures: Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM), Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN), and CNN-LSTM in water level prediction over different time window sizes. We used wind, pressure, and tide data from National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) stations. Our results show that the LSTM model generally outperformed the other models in forecasting water level trends. By applying LSTM, we achieved a mean squared error (MSE) of 0.006, making it the most reliable option for real-world use. We predicted water levels using wind, pressure, and tides. Wind, pressure, and tide data are time-based features that lack spatial patterns. Consequently, LSTM performed better than spatial methods, such as CNN. We also investigated Hurricane Ian, which occurred in Tampa Bay in September 2022 and caused a significant storm surge. Our findings show that CNN and CNN-LSTM performed slightly better than LSTMs during powerful storms, such as hurricanes. Hurricanes are seldom observed in training data, and CNN-based models are more reliable when predicting data that were not included in the training. To explain how environmental factors affect the predicted water level, we used the perturbation method. The perturbation shows that the tide is more effective at predicting water levels than wind and pressure. This study demonstrates the potential of deep learning to improve storm surge prediction accuracy.

title: A global eddy-collocated temperature and salinity profile dataset (v1.0): integrating multiplatform in situ observations with satellite-tracking mesoscale eddies
abstract: We integrated nearly 30 years of global ocean temperature and salinity profile data with satellite mesoscale eddy observations, matching 5.46 million in-situ profiles to adjacent eddies. This dataset enables researchers to characterize the regional three-dimensional eddy structure and investigate how eddies modify ocean thermohaline distributions, alter stratification and mixing, trigger extreme events, drive heat and tracer transport, and respond to climate change.

title: Rainy Season Onset in Central America and the Influence of the ENSO Decaying Phase
abstract: Abstract The description and understanding of physical mechanisms related to delayed rainy season onset in Central America can provide a framework for early warning systems based on a combination of sub-seasonal and seasonal forecasts. This is especially important in regions affected by recurrent rainfall deficits, such as the Central American Dry Corridor. Here, a generalized approach is presented to compute the onset of the rainy season and to analyze physical drivers and their intraseasonal evolution. The independent and joint influences of both the El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO) and the sea-surface temperature of the Tropical North Atlantic (TNA) are discussed by analyzing high-resolution daily rainfall data, moist static stability, vertically-integrated moisture convergence, low-level winds and sea level pressure anomalies for the period 1981–2022. Strongly delayed onsets (more than 7 days) occur over northern Central America in the boreal spring following the peak of El Niño events driven by tropospheric warming due to El Niño, whereas La Niña events tend to modestly hasten the onset due to tropospheric cooling. However, certain regions in northern Central America still experience delays during La Niña. In addition, La Niña events with a warm TNA show significantly delayed onset over the Caribbean side of northern Central America. In this case, onset delay is related to a reduction in surface moisture due to an anomalous low-level circulation likely induced by an extratropical wave-train but not by TNA warming. The results suggest that it is key to consider Pacific-Atlantic basin interactions and their impact on the mid-troposphere when diagnosing rainfall characteristics and rainy season onset in Central America.

title: Value of Adding AI Weather Model Ensembles to a Multi-model Probabilistic Blend
abstract: arXiv:2610.42130v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Many weather forecasting organizations use a multi-model blend of ensemble members from different prediction systems to obtain a more accurate forecast. Recent studies have shown that blending deterministic AI-based models alongside physics-based models improves the overall forecast skill. However, the incorporation of an ensemble AI-based model into a multi-model blend is yet to be investigated. This study explores the value of blending the ensemble version of the Artificial Intelligence Forecasting System (AIFS-CRPS) with the Met Office's convection permitting physics-based ensemble, MOGREPS-UK. We show that blending site temperature (and wind speed) forecasts over the United Kingdom from both ensemble physics-based and ensemble AI-based models leads to an increase in overall forecast skill spatially, across lead times and across exceedance thresholds, especially when the models have different error characteristics. By decomposing the continuous ranked probability score of the blend into component means and diversity terms, we show that a more accurate blend can be achieved by assigning more weight to more skillful models and using models with complementary errors. For example, we show that a blend of MOGREPS-UK with either AIFS-CRPS or the physics-based Integrated Forecasting System (IFS) is better than a blend of IFS and AIFS-CRPS which are not very diverse. This has implications for the importance of weather model diversity and may lend weight to different model development approaches being pursued in tandem. We also demonstrate that calibrating AIFS-CRPS forecasts yields an increase in forecast skill comparable to calibrated ensemble physics-based forecasts, and calibrating the source forecasts before blending and the blended forecast after blending improves the overall forecast accuracy.

title: Stable isotope variability in drip water and its implications for speleothem-based Indian Summer Monsoon reconstruction
abstract: Study region Dandak Cave, located in the Core Monsoon Zone of India. Study focus Understanding the transfer of isotopic composition from precipitation through the karst system to cave drip water is essential for interpreting speleothem-based reconstructions of the Indian Summer Monsoon. Drip water was monitored at three sites in Dandak Cave between 2004 and 2006, with measurements of δ 18 O, δ 13 C, and drip rate conducted to investigate the hydrological and geochemical controls on drip water isotopic composition. The observed drip-water δ 18 O was compared with precipitation δ 18 O estimates from a Rayleigh box model and an isotope-enabled general circulation model ensemble. New hydrological insights for the region Drip water δ 18 O displayed a seasonal cycle, with lower (higher) values during the monsoon (non-monsoon) months, consistent with the seasonal evolution of the estimated precipitation δ 18 O. The relatively small amplitude of drip water δ 18 O compared to that of precipitation suggests attenuation of event-scale variability within the soil–epikarst. Although the three monitoring sites differed in mean drip rate and drip rate variability, their seasonal mean δ 18 O values varied by only 0.1–0.2‰, indicating that they record a similar integrated seasonal signal. δ 13 C varied among sites, reflecting the combined influence of drip hydrology, carbon sources, and cave processes. δ 13 C and radiocarbon analyses yielded limestone-derived carbon contributions of 26 ± 3% and 24 ± 4%, respectively, indicating substantial host-rock carbon input.

title: Rekonstruksi Iklim Purba Miosen Tengah Berdasarkan Studi Palinologi Formasi Lemau Di Seluma, Bengkulu
abstract: AbstrakFosil polen dan spora yang hadir dalam batuan dapat dimanfaatkan untuk merekonstruksi iklim purba saat batuan tersebut diendapkan. Penelitian mengenai iklim purba menggunakan fosil polen dan spora di Pulau Sumatra masih sangat jarang dilakukan. Penelitian ini bertujuan untuk merekonstruksi iklim purba pada Miosen Tengah di Seluma, Bengkulu menggunakan fosil polen dan spora dari Formasi Lemau. Pengambilan sampel menggunakan metode purposive sampling dari penampang stratigrafi terukur dengan interval sampel 5-8 cm. Analisis laboratorium menggunakan metode hidrogen peroksida dan penentuan iklim berdasarkan kehadiran fosil Arboreal Pollen, Non Arboreal Pollen, Graminae, Montane Pollen dan spora. Dari 9 sampel yang dianalisis, menunjukkan 4 zona perubahan dengan dominasi 3 zona berupa iklim hangat dan lembab dan 1 zona dengan iklim hangat dan kelembaban sedang (Zona 3). Selain itu berdasarkan perbandingan kehadiran fosil Arboreal Pollen dan Non Arboreal Pollen, Zona 1 dan Zona 3 menunjukkan kondisi vegetasi tertutup dan Zona 2 dan Zona 4 menunjukkan kondisi vegetasi terbuka. Iklim hangat yang terjadi di daerah penelitian sebagai dampak dari adanya peristiwa global Middle Miocene Climate Optimum (MMCO) dan Middle Miocen Climate Transition (MMCT).AbstractPollen and spore fossils present in rocks can be used to reconstruct the paleoclimate when the rocks were deposited. Research on paleoclimate using pollen and spore fossils on Sumatra Island is still very rare. This study aims to reconstruct the paleoclimate in the Middle Miocene in Bengkulu using pollen and spore fossils from the Lemau Formation. Sampling used a purposive sampling method from measured stratigraphic cross-sections with a sample interval of 5-8 cm. Laboratory analysis used the hydrogen peroxide method and climate determination based on the presence of Arboreal Pollen, Non-Arboreal Pollen, Graminae, Montane Pollen and spore fossils. Of the 9 samples analyzed, it shows 4 change zones with a dominance of 3 zones in the form of a warm and humid climate and 1 zone with a warm and moderate humidity climate (Zone 3). In addition, based on the comparison of the presence of Arboreal Pollen and Non-Arboreal Pollen fossils, Zone 1 and Zone 3 show closed vegetation conditions and Zone 2 and Zone 4 show open vegetation conditions. The warm climate that occurred in the research area was the impact of the global events of the Middle Miocene Climate Optimum (MMCO) and Middle Miocene Climate Transition (MMCT).

title: Decadal strengthening of the preceding-winter ENSO influence on subsequent pre-flood-season precipitation over southern China. Part II: Strengthened La Niña teleconnection due to slower decay and enhanced WES feedback
abstract: Abstract In Part I, we documented a marked mid-1990s strengthening of the ENSO influence on pre-flood-season (PFS; April–June) rainfall over southern China (SC) and identified the dominant mechanism for the strengthened El Niño teleconnection. Here we focus on La Niña and examine why its influence on SC PFS rainfall strengthens after the mid-1990s. Observations show that La Niña events during 1996–2021 (P2) exhibit a slower decay than those during 1959–1995 (P1), allowing cold sea surface temperature (SST) anomalies to persist into AMJ over the Niño4 region and more strongly suppressing central-Pacific convection. The resulting Matsuno–Gill response induces more pronounced low-level wind anomalies over the western North Pacific (WNP). Together with intensified wind–evaporation–SST (WES) coupling in P2, these wind anomalies more effectively modulate surface latent heat fluxes and amplify local SST and convection anomalies over the WNP, exciting a stronger cyclonic circulation spanning the South China Sea and WNP. The associated northeasterly anomalies enhance cold–dry advection over SC, favoring anomalous subsidence and reduced moisture supply and thereby intensifying SC rainfall deficits during La Niña decay years in P2. CMIP6 historical simulations provide complementary support: models with a stronger WES coupling show a stronger La Niña–SC PFS linkage. These results show that the strengthened La Niña teleconnection arises from the combined effects of slower La Niña decay and enhanced WES coupling, providing a phase-dependent counterpart to the El Niño mechanism identified in Part I and highlighting the importance of accurately representing ENSO evolution and WNP air–sea coupling in seasonal prediction of SC PFS rainfall.

title: Evaluating the Behavior of 230 Th and 3 He Constant‐Flux Proxies Across a Carbonate Preservation Gradient in the Cocos Ridge
abstract: Abstract We present a comparison of extraterrestrial 3 He ( 3 He ET ) and excess 230 Th ( 230 Th xs ) as constant flux proxies across a depth transect on the Cocos Ridge, evaluating their behavior as a function of carbonate dissolution and lateral sediment redistribution. Overall, 60% of paired 3 He ET ‐ and 230 Th xs ‐derived mass accumulation rate (MAR) estimates overlap within 1σ uncertainty, indicating broad agreement between the two systems. However, statistically significant discordances between He‐ and Th‐derived MARs occur in three of four cores, with He‐derived MARs exceeding Th‐derived MARs at the ridge crest (positive ΔMAR values) and falling below Th‐derived MARs at flank sites (negative ΔMAR). The discordance at the ridge crest is consistent with sediment winnowing and preferential removal of 3 He‐bearing particles, whereas the smaller discordances in flank cores are best explained by a complementary focusing signal, likely reflecting redistribution of material removed from the ridge top. Evaluation of the negative ΔMAR offsets demonstrates that 230 Th xs is effectively retained during carbonate dissolution, as ΔMAR responses remain small despite strong CaCO 3 preservation gradients, and theoretical constraints indicate negligible thorium mobility. When applied jointly, the two proxies provide complementary constraints on MARs that would remain unresolved using a single proxy. However, their interpretation remains site‐dependent, requiring careful consideration of sediment composition, transport regime, and analytical limitations. Because sedimentary burial fluxes are calculated from component concentrations and MAR, these proxy‐dependent differences directly affect estimates of carbonate and other elemental burial fluxes, with implications for reconstructing both past and modern marine biogeochemical cycles.

title: Calibration guidelines and a runoff-isotope module  for lake proxy system modeling (PRYSM v2.0)
abstract: Lake models are powerful tools for disentangling complex past climate data preserved in sediments. These models can be hard to set-up for lakes that are not well-observed. We improve an existing model with code to simulate water runoff and establish guidelines for setting-up the model when data are scarce. Using our workflow, more scientists can apply this tool to more lakes and gain a better understanding of the climate histories stored in their sediments.

title: Leveraging leaf-level optimality processes with explicit  acclimation improves global GPP representation in  an individual-based DGVM (LPJ-GUESS v4.1.1)
abstract: Global photosynthesis on land is a large flow of carbon in the Earth system which underpins food production and ecosystems. It is particularly important to know how it responds to climate change, but current vegetation models do not agree on this. We implemented a new photosynthesis model based on recent theoretical advances into a vegetation model. We found that it improved the representation of photosynthesis when compared both to global data from satellites and detailed site measurements.

title: OceanTracker 0.5: fast adaptable Lagrangian particle  tracking in structured and unstructured grids
abstract: Ocean currents transport everything from pollution to marine larvae, but tracking millions of virtual particles to understand these movements typically requires weeks of computer processing. OceanTracker solves this bottleneck by being over ten times faster than existing tools, completing million-particle simulations in under an hour on standard computers. This speed breakthrough enables scientists to generate heat maps and analyze connectivity patterns between ocean regions.

title: Including the triple isotopic composition of dissolved  oxygen in the ocean into the iLOVECLIM model  (version 1.1.7): development and evaluation
abstract: The triple isotopic composition of atmospheric oxygen (17Δ) is used to reconstruct past global biospheric productivity. We present the first implementation of the oceanic contribution (17Δocean) in the intermediate-complexity model iLOVECLIM. Photosynthesis, respiration, and air–sea gas exchange are represented under preindustrial conditions. Model results agree with observations, providing a future key tool to study marine biogeochemical processes and past ocean biospheric productivity.

abstract: Physical dynamics of ocean flows at fine spatial scales are challenging for regional and global scale ocean models due to high computational effort associated with smaller grid cell sizes. We compared two ocean models: a regional model (ROMS; Regional Ocean Modeling System) and global model (MPAS-O; Model for Prediction Across Scales – Ocean) across a range of resolutions (10 km to 100 m) in an idealized domain, and found that their similarities may hold promise for future coupling between them.

title: SeidarT: an open-source full-waveform seismic and electromagnetic wave propagation modeling toolbox demonstrated in snow and ice
abstract: We developed open-source software that simulates how elastic and electromagnetic waves travel through snow and ice with the aim to advance and make accessible ice and snow imaging methods. This helps researchers test survey designs and interpret field measurements without expensive or risky expeditions. Parameters influencing the mechanics of snow and ice are easily input from JSON files, and geometries can be generated using an image editor allowing for time effective production of models.

title: Hybrid implicit–explicit XFEM simulation of injection-induced seismicity: resolving multi-scale rupture nucleation and dynamics
abstract: Injecting fluids underground for energy projects can trigger earthquakes. Predicting these events is difficult because underground pressure changes slowly, while faults can move in a fraction of a second. We developed a computer method that switches between two ways of calculating these processes. In our test, it reduced computing time by 62 % while giving similar estimates of earthquake size and total fault movement. Differences in the fastest movements show that further testing is needed.

title: Slope-Constrained Orography (SCO v1.0) for explicit discrete-slope control in terrain preprocessing: a case study with WRF-ARW (v4.6.1)
abstract: High-resolution weather models over mountains need terrain smoothing to avoid crashing, but standard methods smooth everywhere regardless of need. We developed Slope-Constrained Orography, a tool that uses one slope-angle setting to adjust only the points that are too steep. Tested over the southeastern Tibetan Plateau, stable simulations were achieved while modifying far less terrain than standard smoothing, offering a simpler approach to running weather models over steep terrain.

title: GECKO-A v1.0: exploring VOC oxidation trajectories through comparison with the master chemical mechanism
abstract: This study presents the first open-source release of a tool that automatically generates chemical mechanisms for the atmospheric oxidation of organic compounds. Simulations for five hydrocarbons, under conditions ranging from urban to remote, are compared with a benchmark mechanism. Results show that describing successive oxidation steps is key to simulating the formation of low-volatility and water-soluble species important for aerosols. A reduced mechanism reproduces most of these results.
